classification.difficultyReason: Infer preserved perpendicularity from the fold, select corresponding exposed triangles, and link Pythagoras to similarity. Generalise the argument algebraically and explain how successive constructions reach every unit fraction.

content.prompt: It is easy to fold a piece of paper perfectly in half. But can you fold it into perfect thirds? Or quarters? Or fifths? We show that you can fold a piece of paper exactly into any unit fraction you wish.

inlines.text: Take a square piece of paper and mark half way along the top side with a small crease. Now fold the bottom left corner to meet this halfway mark and crease the paper.

spec.description: Folded unit square; light purple exposed paper and light blue folded flap. The flap extends beyond the right edge.
spec.mathematics: Top halves 1/2; exposed left length x; rotated left edge 1−x; exposed right length y. Fold preserves lengths and perpendicularity.
spec.answerVisibility: No solution labels or computed lengths.

children.prompt: In the figure above, prove that $y=\dfrac23$. This means that we can fold a length of $\dfrac13$ by folding length $y$ in half.

answer.short:
$y=\dfrac23$.

Pythagoras gives $x=\dfrac38$; corresponding sides of the two exposed right triangles give $y$.
answer.worked:
Name the top left corner $A$, top midpoint $B$, top right corner $C$, left crease endpoint $E$, and the intersection of the sloping flap edge with the right edge $D$. In right triangle $ABE$,
$$\begin{align*}x^2+\left(\frac12\right)^2&=(1-x)^2,\\x^2+\frac14&=1-2x+x^2,\\2x&=\frac34,\\x&=\frac38.\end{align*}$$
The fold preserves the right angle between $BE$ and $BD$. Thus $\triangle ABE\sim\triangle CDB$ by AAA: both have a right angle, and their remaining angles match because $AB\perp CD$ and $BE\perp DB$.
$$\begin{align*}\frac{AB}{CD}&=\frac{AE}{CB},\\\frac{1/2}{y}&=\frac{3/8}{1/2},\\\frac1{2y}&=\frac34,\\y&=\frac23.\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Now suppose we can fold the length $\dfrac1n$.

spec.description: Generalised folded unit square, shown schematically with the top fold point left of centre; semantic paper-region fills match part (a).
spec.mathematics: Top segments 1/n and 1−1/n; left segment x; rotated edge 1−x; right exposed segment y. Geometry uses an illustrative n=3 without displaying that value.
spec.answerVisibility: Only given symbolic lengths; no solution labels.

children.prompt: In the figure above, prove that $y=\dfrac{2}{n+1}$. Note that this means that we can fold length $\dfrac1{n+1}$ by folding length $y$ in half.

answer.short:
$y=\dfrac{2}{n+1}$.

Repeat part (a) with top lengths $\dfrac1n$ and $1-\dfrac1n$.
answer.worked:
Use the same point names as in part (a), with $AB=\frac{1}{n}$ and $CB=1-\frac{1}{n}$. Pythagoras in $\triangle ABE$ gives
$$\begin{align*}x^2+\frac1{n^2}&=(1-x)^2,\\x^2+\frac1{n^2}&=1-2x+x^2,\\2x&=1-\frac1{n^2},\\x&=\frac{n^2-1}{2n^2}.\end{align*}$$
As in part (a), $\triangle ABE\sim\triangle CDB$ by AAA. Therefore
$$\begin{align*}\frac{AB}{CD}&=\frac{AE}{CB},\\\frac{1/n}{y}&=\frac{x}{1-1/n},\\y&=\frac{n-1}{n^2x},\\y&=\frac{2(n-1)}{n^2-1},\\y&=\frac2{n+1}.\end{align*}$$
Halving this length constructs $\frac{1}{(n+1)}$.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Why does this mean that we can construct any unit fraction?

answer.short: Start with $\dfrac12$. Part (a) constructs $\dfrac13$, and repeated use of part (b) constructs $\dfrac14$, $\dfrac15$, and every subsequent unit fraction.
answer.worked: A half can be folded directly. Part (a) constructs a third. Whenever $\frac{1}{n}$ has been constructed, part (b) constructs $\frac{1}{(n+1)}$. Repeating this step reaches every positive integer denominator, so every unit fraction can be constructed.
